Guided Inquiry

1 · Meet the ceiling

An engine sits between a hot reservoir at T_H = 600 K and a cold one at T_C = 300 K. It absorbs Q_H = 1000 J each cycle. Watch the three streams: heat in from the hot side, work out, heat rejected to the cold side. Their widths are drawn to scale.

Press Play and let the PV cycle trace once. Then move on.

2 · Predict — which lever helps more?

You want a more efficient engine. Starting from T_H = 600 K, T_C = 300 K, which single change raises the efficiency more?

3 · Verify — try both

Move T_H from 600 K to 700 K. Read η. Then reset it, and move T_C from 300 K to 200 K instead. Read η again. The cold-side change is the bigger win, every time.

Notice that the green (work) stream widens and the blue (rejected) stream narrows — but the blue one never closes.

4 · Predict — could a perfect engine reject nothing?

An advertisement claims an engine that converts all its heat to work — Q_C = 0, η = 1. Which of these must be true for that to be possible?

5 · The signature of reversibility

Look at the entropy readout below. For the Carnot cycle the hot reservoir loses exactly the entropy the cold one gains, so ΔS_total = 0 — the only cycle for which that is true. Every real engine produces some entropy and falls short of this bound.

Move the sliders freely. The efficiency will change with T_H and T_C, but ΔS_total will stay pinned to zero — that is Carnot's signature.

The Physics

The Carnot Cycle — the Ceiling No Engine Can Beat · what this sim shows, the physics behind it, and every control

01

At a glance

A Carnot engine sits between a hot reservoir and a cold one. Each cycle it takes in heat, turns some of it into work and passes the rest to the cold side. The sim draws those three flows as streams and shows the gas tracing a loop on a PV diagram.

What you'll learn

  • How the heat taken in, the work done and the heat rejected balance each cycle.
  • How the four legs of the PV loop are built from two isotherms and two adiabats.
  • What sets an engine's efficiency, and what the entropy readout is checking.
Heat flows in from the hot side, work leaves, and the rest of the heat goes to the cold side.

What's on screen

  • Energy flow (left): the two reservoirs, the engine, and three streams: amber for heat in, green for work out, blue for heat rejected.
  • PV diagram (right): the four-leg loop with a moving dot, and the name of the leg underneath.
  • Read panel (sidebar): the efficiency η and the total entropy change ΔStotal.
See itRun the engine with its starting reservoirs. Watch for: an amber stream into the engine, green and blue streams leaving it, and a dot circling the PV loop.

03

Heat in, work out and heat rejected balance every cycle

After one full cycle the gas is back in its starting state, so its internal energy has not changed. The first law then says that the net heat taken in equals the work done, QH − QC = W, or

QH = W + QC
QH is heat from the hot reservoir, W is work out, QC is heat passed to the cold reservoir. All three are counted as positive amounts.

The sim fixes QH at 1000 J and draws each stream as wide as its energy. Put the green and blue streams side by side and they are exactly as wide as the amber one, because no energy is created or lost.

The efficiency is the share of the heat paid in that comes back as work, η = W / QH.

See itCompare the stream widths. Watch for: the green and blue streams together being as wide as the amber one.
04

The PV loop has two isotherms and two adiabats

Starting at point 1, the gas goes through four legs, and the sim names the current one under the diagram:

  • 1 → 2, isothermal expansion at TH: the gas absorbs QH from the hot reservoir.
  • 2 → 3, adiabatic expansion: no heat flows, and the gas cools from TH to TC.
  • 3 → 4, isothermal compression at TC: the gas gives QC to the cold reservoir.
  • 4 → 1, adiabatic compression: no heat flows, and the gas warms back to TH.

The area enclosed by the loop is the net work W per cycle. The two isotherms stretch the volume by the same factor, V2/V1 = V3/V4 (both 3 in the sim), and that is what lets the two adiabats close the loop.

The loop is qualitative: it uses arbitrary units on fixed axes. When TH/TC goes above about 3.5, point 3 runs past the edge of the plot, but the streams and readouts stay correct.

See itFollow the dot round the loop. Watch for: the leg name under the diagram changing as the dot passes through each corner.
05

Efficiency is set by the temperature ratio

For a reversible engine between reservoirs at TH and TC, measured in kelvin:

η = W / QH = 1 − TC / TH
No engine working between the same two reservoirs can do better than this Carnot value.

Only the ratio TC/TH matters. At 600 K and 300 K it is 1/2, so half of QH becomes work: W = 500 J, QC = 500 J, and η = 0.500. Double both temperatures to 1200 K and 600 K and the ratio, and so η, does not change.

When the reservoirs are close the engine is poor. At 310 K and 300 K, η is only 0.032.

See itSet both reservoirs to twice their starting values. Watch for: 1200 K and 600 K with η = 0.500, W = 500 J and QC = 500 J, as before.
06

Lowering the cold temperature helps more than raising the hot one

Start from 600 K and 300 K. Lowering TC by 100 K to 200 K lifts η from 0.500 to 0.667, a gain of 0.167. Raising TH by 100 K to 700 K lifts it only to 0.571, a gain of 0.071.

For small steps, one kelvin taken off TC raises η by 1/TH, while one kelvin added to TH raises it by TC/TH2. The first is bigger by the factor TH/TC, which is 2 at the start and is always above 1.

In practice the cold side is usually the surroundings and is hard to cool, so real engines are improved mostly by running hotter.

See itLower TC to 200 K. Watch for: η = 0.667, W = 667 J and the blue stream narrowing to 333 J.
See itRaise TH to 700 K instead. Watch for: η = 0.571, W = 571 J and QC = 429 J, a smaller gain.
07

A perfect engine needs a cold reservoir at 0 K

Setting η = 1 in η = 1 − TC/TH gives TC/TH = 0, so TC = 0 K. Then QC = 0 and all of QH becomes work.

Friction and the choice of working substance do not enter, because the limit comes from the two temperatures alone. Making TH huge does not help either, since TC/TH gets small but never reaches zero. Absolute zero cannot be reached in a finite number of steps (the third law), so η = 1 is never achieved.

The sim shows this at its limit. With TH = 1200 K and TC = 1 K, η is 0.999, but a thin blue stream of about 1 J still leaves for the cold reservoir.

See itPush TH to 1200 K and TC to 1 K. Watch for: η = 0.999, yet the blue stream is still there, with a note that QC > 0.
08

Entropy out of the hot side equals entropy into the cold side

A reservoir that gives up heat Q at temperature T loses entropy Q/T, and one that receives heat gains Q/T. The gas returns to its starting state each cycle, so only the reservoirs change:

ΔStotal = −QH/TH + QC/TC = 0
At the starting values the hot side loses 1.667 J/K and the cold side gains 1.667 J/K.

Setting this to zero gives QC/QH = TC/TH, which is the efficiency formula again. Zero total entropy change is the signature of a reversible cycle.

A real engine creates entropy, so ΔStotal > 0. It rejects more heat and delivers less work than the Carnot engine. The sim models only the reversible engine, so its readout is 0.000 J/K at every setting.

See itSet TH to 900 K, TC stays at 300 K. Watch for: ΔStotal = 0.000 J/K even though η has changed to 0.667.
09

Summary

In one line. A Carnot engine splits each cycle's heat into work and rejected heat, and the two reservoir temperatures decide how that split falls.

Key points

  • QH = W + QC, and η = W/QH = 1 − TC/TH in kelvin.
  • A kelvin off TC is worth TH/TC times a kelvin added to TH.
  • η = 1 needs TC = 0 K, and ΔStotal = 0 marks a reversible cycle.

Common mix-ups

  • "Better materials could make QC zero." The limit comes from the temperatures, not the engine.
  • "Celsius values can go in the formula." Use 300 K and 600 K, not 27 °C and 327 °C, or η comes out as 0.92 instead of 0.50.
  • "Only the temperature gap matters." The ratio matters: 1200 K and 600 K give the same η as 600 K and 300 K.

Things to try on your own

  • Find the TC that gives η = 0.75 at TH = 600 K, then check it in the sim.
  • Check that W + QC adds up to 1000 J at three different settings.
